Discharge always means: something being released, let out, sent away, or completed. That "something" can be a person, a substance, energy, or an obligation. Once you grasp this single idea — a release or an outflow — every meaning of this word will make sense instantly.

1. The Official Release of a Person

When someone is formally let go from a place or institution, that act is called a discharge.

  • A patient leaving the hospital after treatment → hospital discharge
  • A soldier leaving the army at the end of service → military discharge
  • A prisoner being freed after serving their sentence → discharge from prison

There are different kinds of military discharge based on how well the soldier served:

  • An honourable discharge means the soldier served well and is leaving with a good record.
  • A dishonourable discharge means the soldier was removed for serious misconduct — it carries lasting consequences.

"He received his discharge from the army after twenty years of service."

2. The Flow or Release of a Substance

This meaning covers anything — liquid, gas, or waste — that flows out of something.

In medicine: Discharge refers to fluid coming out of the body, especially from a wound, an eye, the nose, or other openings. This is often an important clinical sign.

"The doctor noticed a yellowish discharge from the wound — a sign of infection."

In industry and environment: When a factory or a pipe releases chemicals or waste into a river or the air, that release is called a discharge.

"The company was fined for the illegal discharge of toxic chemicals into the river."

In hydrology (the science of water): Discharge measures how much water is flowing through a river at a given point — usually expressed in cubic metres per second. A river after heavy rain has a high discharge.

"The discharge of the Ganges increases dramatically during monsoon season."

3. The Release of Electrical Energy

When electricity stored somewhere is suddenly released, that event is a discharge.

  • Lightning is a massive electrical discharge between clouds and the ground.
  • When you touch a metal doorknob and feel a small shock after walking on carpet, that tiny spark is an electrostatic discharge.
  • A battery that has used up all its stored energy has undergone full discharge.

"The static discharge from the equipment damaged the sensitive circuit board."

4. The Firing of a Weapon

When a gun or any firearm is fired — whether intentionally or accidentally — the act of firing is called a discharge.

"The accidental discharge of the weapon injured a bystander."

This meaning comes from the idea of the gun releasing the bullet and the built-up gas pressure inside. The same word is used for cannons, rifles, and any kind of firearm.

5. The Completion of a Duty or Obligation

This is a more formal, legal or professional meaning. When someone fulfils a responsibility — they carry it out fully and are now free of it — that is called the discharge of that duty or obligation.

Think of it this way: before you do your duty, it sits on your shoulders. Once you have fully done it, it is released from you. That release is the discharge.

"The board praised him for the faithful discharge of his duties over thirty years."
"The repayment of the loan represented the discharge of his financial obligation."

In bankruptcy law, a debt discharge is a court ruling that frees a person from the legal obligation to repay certain debts. The creditor can no longer pursue that money. This is one of the most significant legal meanings of the word.

"After declaring bankruptcy, she was granted a discharge of her remaining debts."

6. The Dismissal of a Legal Case

In a court of law, if a judge decides that a case should be dropped — often because the evidence is too weak or the accusation does not meet the legal standard — the dismissal of the accused is called a discharge.

"The judge ordered the discharge of the accused due to insufficient evidence."

This is different from a "not guilty" verdict — a discharge often means the case never properly proceeded to a full trial.
How to Tell the Meanings Apart

Since the word appears in so many fields, the context will almost always tell you which meaning is intended:

  • Hospital, clinic, patient → release of a person from medical care
  • Military, army, service record → formal separation from armed forces
  • Wound, body, fluid → bodily fluid coming out
  • River, factory, pipe, environment → outflow of water or waste
  • Electricity, battery, static, spark → release of electrical energy
  • Gun, firearm, weapon → the act of firing
  • Duty, responsibility, obligation → the fulfilment of a task
  • Court, judge, charges, accused → dismissal of a legal case
  • Debt, bankruptcy, creditor → legal release from financial obligation
The One Thread That Connects Everything

No matter which meaning you encounter, ask yourself: what is being released here, and from where?

  • A patient is released from the hospital.
  • A soldier is released from military service.
  • Fluid is released from a wound.
  • Water is released from a river channel.
  • Electricity is released from a cloud or a battery.
  • A bullet is released from a gun.
  • A person is released from a legal or financial obligation.

That single image — something breaking free, flowing out, or being formally let go — is the soul of the word discharge.
